new_statements.quote: [p.132] In Mro five of the TB *prefixes are realized or preserved, but only three of them have remained separable and functional. All five of them show an open transition between the prefixed element and the following consonant/consonant cluster of the verb or noun root. Daai mna 'buffalo' and Mro mna 'buffalo' are written alike in the practical orthography, but in Mro 'buffalo' is pronounced [mə na]. ... [pp.136-137] Eventually I made a surprising discovery: Mro has yet another prefix, ka-, that is phonetically very distinct from k- [kə-]. It is an unstressed prefix, or pre-syllable, but with the distinct vowel [a~ʌ]. ... Prefixed ka- occurs only with verb roots.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Mro (= Mro-Khimi, Wakung) is a tone language (Hornéy 2012: two contrastive tones H/L, melodies on the root, affixes toneless). Words are (CV-)(Cə-)ROOT(-CV): prefixes are either schwa presyllables (m-, t-, k-, s-, x- with a short epenthetic [ə]) or the full-vowel prefix ka- (and ʔa-), and So-Hartmann explicitly calls ka- 'an unstressed prefix, or pre-syllable' like the schwa presyllables; prominence therefore sits on the root (major) syllable that follows the prefixes - the iambic presyllable + stressed main-syllable pattern she describes for Southern Chin (2009: 36-38, with Mro cognates). No source states a syllable-counting stress rule or says anything about stress on suffixes/enclitics beyond their being toneless.
new_statements.exceptions: None as such; ka- differs from the schwa presyllables only in keeping a full vowel [a~ʌ] while still unstressed. Hornéy 2012:39 adds that the minor-syllable schwa 'has a much shorter duration than vowels in other syllables' and cannot bear lexical tone.
new_statements.domain_note: Statement concerns prefix + root words (verbs and nouns) in citation/wordlist and text data from Kyauktaw-township Mro (So-Hartmann's consultant U Kyaw Tha Aung); it is a remark within a morphophonological article on prefixes, not a dedicated stress section. Hornéy's fuller phonology (Wakun dialect) is silent on stress, so the combined picture is: tonal, sesquisyllabic, root-prominent, prefixes unstressed.
new_statements.identity_note: khum1250 'Khumi Awa Chin' [cka] is a retired ISO entity merged in 2012 into Mro-Khimi Chin [cmr] (Glottolog mroc1235 'Mro Chin'). ISO CR 2011-037 identifies 'Awa Khami' with the Wakung ('downstream') sub-group of Mro-Khimi; So-Hartmann 1988:101 ('Wakung.. also called Awa Khama') and 2009:25 ('Wakung is.. a major subgroup of Mro') agree. Both sources used here describe exactly this variety: So-Hartmann 2001's 'Mro' is the Wakung/Mro-Khimi of Paletwa-Kyauktaw (p.132, explicitly 'not the Khimi language Shafer dealt with'), and Hornéy 2012 analyses the Wakun dialect (4 of 5 consultants, plus one Xautau speaker). Any catalog entry should be filed under mroc1235 (Mro-Khimi), with khum1250 as a bookkeeping alias; it must not be conflated with Khumi proper [cnk] (khum1248, Peterson's Bangladesh Khumi) or Eastern/Lemi/Kanise Khumi [cek] (east2779).

sources.note: p.132: Mro prefixes s-/sh-, m-, t-, k-, x- 'show an open transition between the prefixed element and the following consonant' ([mə na] 'buffalo'); pp.136-137 (page images verified): 'Mro has yet another prefix, ka-, that is phonetically very distinct from k- [kə-]. It is an unstressed prefix, or pre-syllable, but with the distinct vowel [a~ʌ].' p.124 (about Daai): 'The syllabic nasals and syllabic [ʔ] are unstressed syllables'. I.e. prefixes/presyllables are unstressed relative to the root; no fuller rule.

sources.note: Second-hand summaries of Hornéy 2012 on Mro Khimi (minor syllables underlyingly vowelless, schwa 'much shorter', minor-syllable tone post-lexical, prefixes polar tone) and Tan 2022:41 quotes the So-Hartmann 2001:136-137 'unstressed prefix' sentence for Mro Khimi /ka-/. These works are about Kanise Khumi [cek], not this variety.

sources.note: About Daai, with Mro comparison: p.36 phonological word = optional unstressed presyllable + stressed main syllable, 'IAMBIC stress contour'; p.38 compares Mro cognates mə.ju 'suck', mə.lœ 'vomit', mə.sʰu 'launder': 'the reduction of the presyllable takes different degrees, with Daai being the most reduced.. and Mro and Lemi having a bit more syllabicity in the form of a reduced schwa vowel'. p.25: 'Wakung is.. a major subgroup of Mro' (identity). p.31: Shafer 1944 'Khimi' is Khumi (St Matthew by E.W. Francis), not Mro-Khimi.

sources.note: The word 'stress' never occurs. Ch.4: three syllable types - major [C(C)V], minor-syllable prefixes [Cə] whose inserted schwa 'has a much shorter duration than vowels in other syllables' (p.39), full prefixes [CV] (ʔɑ-, kɑ-); maximal word [CV.Cə.CCV.CV] (p.41). Ch.5: two contrastive tones H/L, four root melodies H L LH HL; affixes underlyingly toneless (suffixes get root tone by spreading, prefixes polar tone); falling pitch only phrase-final (pp.43, 58). No statement of stress/accent placement.
